title: Fieldwork
examples: What is the difference between collecting primary and secondary data?
How do I make sure my hypothesis is testable?
Can I use maps as evidence in my fieldwork report?

explain.say: Today we are learning about fieldwork in geography.
First, you must form a clear hypothesis for your study.

items: It must relate to your topic.
It must be testable in the field.

explain.say: For example, you might predict that slope affects litter size.
Next, you need to collect reliable data from the location.
A concrete example is using quadrats to measure plant density.
Finally, you must evaluate all the data you have gathered.

faq.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary data?
faq.a: Primary data is information you collect yourself during fieldwork. Secondary data is information that already exists, like from books or websites.
asks: Where do I find secondary data?
Is using old maps considered primary data?

faq.q: How do I make sure my hypothesis is testable?
faq.a: Your hypothesis must make a clear prediction that you can measure in the real world. If you cannot measure it, it is not testable.
asks: Does 'it might be' make a good hypothesis?

faq.q: What is a quadrat used for in fieldwork?
faq.a: A quadrat is a square frame used to estimate the density of plants or organisms in a specific area. You count what is inside it.
asks: How many quadrats should I use?

faq.q: What does 'evaluation' mean in a fieldwork report?
faq.a: Evaluation means judging the quality of your work. You must discuss what was good about your methods and what problems you faced.
asks: Do I just say what went wrong?
Is evaluation the same as conclusion?

faq.q: Can I use rainfall data from a weather station?
faq.a: Yes, that is an example of secondary data. You are using information someone else has already recorded.
asks: Is a graph of historical temperature secondary data?

faq.q: If my hypothesis is 'pollution is bad', is that okay?
faq.a: No, that is too general. You need to predict a specific relationship, like 'increased pollution causes a decrease in bird numbers.'
asks: Should my hypothesis include the word 'because'?

faq.a: You should discuss limitations during the evaluation stage. This shows you understand the real-world challenges of fieldwork.
asks: Is discussing limitations the same as suggesting improvements?
Do I need to list every single problem?

facts: A hypothesis is a testable prediction about a relationship.
Primary data is collected directly by the researcher in the field.
Evaluation involves judging the reliability and validity of your data.
Quadrats are square frames used to sample vegetation density.

quiz.say: A student predicts that the closer a river is to a town, the more pollution it will have. This prediction is a:
quiz.why: It is a clear, testable prediction about a relationship between two variables.

wrong.0: An observation is just a single piece of information seen, not a full prediction.
wrong.2: A conclusion is what you state after analyzing the data, not before.
wrong.3: Data are the measurements you take; a hypothesis is the idea you are testing.

quiz.say: You measure the height of trees at several spots using a measuring tape. This measurement is an example of:
quiz.why: You collected this measurement yourself at the site, making it primary data.

wrong.1: Secondary data comes from sources like textbooks or official records.
wrong.2: A hypothesis is a guess, not the actual measurement you record.
wrong.3: Evaluation happens later when you judge the quality of these measurements.

quiz.say: When evaluating your fieldwork, you notice that it rained heavily during your sampling time. This point should be discussed as a:
quiz.why: A limitation describes a weakness or constraint that affected your ability to collect perfect data.

wrong.0: The conclusion is your final answer, not a comment on the process.
wrong.1: The hypothesis is what you set out to test at the very beginning.
wrong.2: An observation is a fact; a limitation is a discussion about the quality of the data.
